# Agentic Tasks with `yantra do`

`yantra do "<goal>"` runs a governed web agent that can research, browse, fill forms, invoke saved workflows, and publish a validated task Brief. It is for browser and public-web work that needs several decisions or actions, while keeping model access, website access, consent, secrets, and artifacts inside Yantra's enforced boundaries.

## What It Does

Each goal that passes deterministic input, credential, and location preflight creates one auditable Yantra run and one fresh model-provider session. The agent receives the goal, authoritative date/time/locale context, any granted user location, approved personalization, and only Yantra's registered tools. The runtime owns the reasoning loop, tool policy, budgets, publication requirement, and teardown; the CLI streams progress and renders the terminal outcome. A location preflight handoff is also recorded as a run, but opens no provider session.

The governed scope rules keep the run on the requested task. The agent may choose how to accomplish a broad goal, but it must not add unrequested actions, substitute values found on a page for values the user supplied, retry an adverse outcome with different inputs, or run side experiments to explain a surprising result. Verification means checking that the requested action landed, not investigating beyond the goal.

The prompt is versioned as `agent-v10` (recorded as `prompt_version` in `manifest.json`). It retains the governed scope rules and adds publication guidance for cited findings, tables, conditions, and unmet requirements. Beyond the scope rules above, it tells the agent:

- **Source fidelity.** When the goal names a source, the fields it wants, or conditions the results must meet, those are part of what it asks: deliver from that source, and for each condition either confirm it in the evidence or report it as unconfirmed, never state it as met because the goal asked for it.
- **No unreported causes.** Never explain missing data with a cause no tool result reported; say the evidence did not contain it.
- **Following an offered link is progress.** The agent may try at most one materially different fallback (for example, other sites than the goal names), but following a link or listing that a result already offered is progress on the direct approach, not a fallback.

The per-run prompt's scope line is derived from the run's actual tool catalog, so it never claims a capability the session lacks:

- No browser tool (`research --no-browse`): "Scope: web search and page reading only; this run has no live browser."
- Read-only browser tools only (`research`): "Scope: web search, page reading, and read-only browsing (navigate, observe, extract); this run cannot click or fill forms — if the goal needs that, report it and name `yantra do` as the next step."
- Any click or fill tool (`do`): "Scope: browser and web work only."

The `do` completion criteria also carry the required-source rule (when the goal names a site or source, read the answer from it and present any other source only as a clearly labeled alternative, never merged into the answer) and ask the agent to call `task_contract` in the same turn as its first search or fetch. The `research` guidance is described in [Research](research.md#agentic-research).

The `do` profile exposes these capabilities:

| Capability                         | Current behavior                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Public-web research                | Searches the web and fetches readable content from the top results, or with `limit: 0` returns only titles, URLs, and snippets. It can fetch one specific public link already supplied, returned by a search, or offered by a page already read, subject to URL and ethics policy. Every read reports the page's shape and returns its records, tables, fields, structured data, and links. Each page is fetched at most once per run and keeps one evidence ID. |
| Browser navigation and observation | Lazily opens system Chrome in a fresh run-scoped profile, follows policy-approved URLs, and returns bounded page text plus opaque references for visible controls.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Browser actions                    | Clicks observed controls and fills text, autocomplete suggestions, native choices, toggles, ISO dates, and date ranges. Multi-field forms are filled together and verified before the agent submits them separately.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Page extraction                    | Extracts the live page's readable content, records, links, schema.org structured data, every table, or one table by index, through the same analyzer `web_fetch` uses. Large results become run-local capture references instead of being placed fully in model context.                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Saved workflows                    | Lists and runs a matching saved workflow through the deterministic executor. The nested workflow gets its own run directory and opens no second model session.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Task contract                      | Records what the goal requires (deliverable, fields, filters, required sites) as `contract.json` and echoes it to the user. Optional; see [Task contract](#task-contract).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Data transformations               | Runs only the built-in, allowlisted transformations `table_normalize`, `dedupe_lines`, and `json_pick`; it cannot execute arbitrary code or shell commands.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Publication                        | Publishes exactly one validated Brief, including cited findings, sections, and table rows, or one report shaped by a selected template. The Brief distinguishes sources cited in the answer from pages also consulted.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

Browser actions return a fresh observation after the page settles, so the agent can continue without a redundant read. Opaque element references remain usable on the same document and are invalidated when a new document loads. If a site opens a same-site results tab, Yantra policy-checks it and follows it as the run's page. Cross-site or non-HTTP(S) popups are closed and reported so the agent can navigate explicitly when policy permits.

**Every action also reports what changed, not only what the page looks like now.** `browser_click`, `browser_navigate`, `browser_fill_element`, and `browser_fill_form` return a compact `delta` block **alongside** the existing `observation` — additive, not a replacement, so anything that read the observation before reads exactly the same now. `browser_observe` is deliberately unchanged: it is a read without an action, so there is no action window to describe. `browser_fill_form` returns one `delta` for the whole call rather than one per field, spanning the page the agent last saw to the page the batch left behind.

Every field is omitted when there is nothing to say, so an action that changed nothing produces a near-empty block:

| Field                                    | Meaning                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `url_changed`                            | The `from` and `to` addresses.                                                                                                                   |
| `title_changed`                          | The `from` and `to` document titles.                                                                                                             |
| `dialogs_opened`, `dialogs_closed`       | Containers observed opening or closing, each a `{role, name}` pair in the same vocabulary the obstruction report uses for an overlay's identity. |
| `elements_appeared`, `elements_vanished` | A definite `count`, a capped named `sample`, and `sample_truncated` when the sample names fewer controls than the count.                         |
| `focus_moved`                            | The `from` and `to` controls, named the same way; a side is omitted when focus was not on a scanned control.                                     |

**A delta says what changed in the action window, not that the action caused it.** A page that mounts a banner on a timer shortly after a click contributes to the delta exactly as the click's own effects do, and nothing in the signal separates them. It also lists dialogs it observed opening or closing and never asserts that no dialog is open — a container is nameable only when it holds at least one scanned control, so silence about dialogs is silence rather than an all-clear.

**Where a bound prevents a definite statement, the block says so instead of manufacturing a number.** It then carries `complete: false` together with an `incomplete` list drawn from a fixed set: `document-replaced` (the two frames are different documents, so element counts and focus are omitted — a new document's controls are not the old document's), `fingerprint-truncated`, and `scan-degraded`. With no prior model-visible observation there is nothing to diff, so the block is omitted entirely; that is the ordinary state of a run's first navigation.

**The delta is computed over an uncapped semantic fingerprint, which is what makes it true.** Refs are minted from role, name, and ordinal, and the model-visible list is capped at 50 elements, so a delta derived from what the agent sees would routinely report appearances and vanishings that never happened. Each frame is instead fingerprinted by role, accessible name, group, and scope during the scan the observation was already performing. The observed consequences: same-named controls that merely reorder are not reported as appearing and vanishing, a control set the page remounts identically reports no change at all, and an element pushed past the model-visible cap is not reported as vanished.

**It costs no extra page read.** One action still takes exactly one post-action observation, and the fingerprint is derived inside it. Derivation is best-effort: a post-action read that fails degrades to no observation and no delta rather than turning an action that already succeeded into a tool error.

**A popup, a JS dialog, or a landing URL produced by a fill is now reported on that fill's result.** Such events were previously dropped or surfaced on whatever tool ran next, and `browser_navigate` would then refuse, as `URL_NOT_FROM_EVIDENCE`, the very URL a fill had just navigated to. Both fill tools now record URL provenance the way `browser_click` already did — where the fill landed, and any intercepted popup's target — so navigating back to a URL a fill produced is no longer refused as an unattested guess. A same-site tab a fill opened is policy-checked and followed exactly as on the click path, with `switched_to_new_tab` reported and the post-action observation and delta taken on the adopted page. A cross-site popup is still closed and reported as `popup_intercepted`, and a tab the ethics gate refuses is left unadopted with the rest of the result unchanged.

Observation walks the composed tree, so a control a page encapsulates inside a component's own **open** shadow root is scanned, named, given an `eNN` ref, and clicked or filled like any other interactable. This is a property of observation itself, so it holds for every browser tool, and nothing about the ref contract, the observation payload, or the tool arguments differs for such a control. A **closed** shadow root stays unreachable by design: the platform withholds that subtree from the page, so the control is simply absent from the observation and there is nothing to address. No piercing library and no DOM tagging is used to get around that.

Form filling uses one deterministic engine for ordinary controls and stateful widgets. `browser_fill_form` fills up to ten non-secret fields in order and never submits the form.

**A field that fails no longer ends the batch.** A four-field call that stopped on the first failure returned nothing applied — a call that existed to make four fields' worth of progress made none, and the three untouched fields were indistinguishable from three that had been tried and refused. Every remaining field is now attempted, and the result carries three sets:

| Set       | Meaning                                                                                                                                     |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `applied` | Fields that landed, each with `requested`, `committed`, and `resolution` as a single fill reports them.                                     |
| `failed`  | Fields that were attempted and did not take, each with `observed`, `attempted`, and genuine `offered` choices when the widget exposes them. |
| `skipped` | Fields not attempted, with `blocked_by` naming the failed field that blocks them.                                                           |
| `covers`  | Optional on an entry in any set; lists every caller field that one fused fill accounts for when it stands for more than its named `field`.  |

Every field sent appears exactly once across those sets, read as `entry.covers ?? [entry.field]`. A date range that the page commits as one unit therefore remains one truthful entry in `applied`, `failed`, or `skipped`, while `covers` names both caller fields it represents. A covering failure's `requested` value reports the composite range it drove; it does not claim which endpoint failed because that information is not present in the failure contract. A field named in `covers` is already accounted for; do not re-send it as missing, and when that entry fails, resolve the covered fields together.

A field is skipped only when it belongs to the same widget as one that failed — a shared range picker, or one overlay — because a second attempt there would fail for a reason the caller cannot tell apart from a real problem with that field. Resolve the blocking field first. Dependence is read from the widget grouping the page itself reports, never from the order the fields were listed in.

The call succeeds when **any** field applied, so a partial result is progress to build on rather than a reason to re-send the fields that worked; it fails only when nothing applied at all. A partial batch is also visible in the run's audit trail: `report.md` renders it as `partial (N applied, N failed, N skipped)` rather than as a flat `ok`. `browser_fill_element` handles a single field and is the only fill path for a host-bound stored website secret. Successful fills verify the committed state; ambiguity, stale controls, incomplete date ranges, or values that do not commit return typed failures instead of guessed success.

Field names are resolved conservatively. A first-time request whose repeated accessible-label matches remain tied after safe narrowing returns `FORM_FIELD_AMBIGUOUS` instead of choosing by document order; the failure identifies each candidate by ref, accessible name, role, and group so the caller can address the intended control. Document order is available only while re-acquiring a control that was already identified, and only when the candidates preserve that prior identity and share the same normalized name, role, and group. Repeated labels in different forms, cards, rows, or dialogs therefore remain ambiguous.

**A fill reports how its value was resolved.** A widget frequently commits something other than what was typed — a location field asked for an airport code offers a city name and stores that. The committed value is the fact, and the result says how it came about rather than leaving the agent to guess whether its fill worked:

| Field        | Meaning                                                                                                                              |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `requested`  | What the caller asked for, as it was expressed.                                                                                      |
| `committed`  | What the control holds now.                                                                                                          |
| `resolution` | How the two relate — see below.                                                                                                      |
| `offered`    | Genuine choices the widget exposed, up to ten pairwise-distinct labels; omitted when a failed container exposes no option semantics. |
| `note`       | One sentence, present when `committed` differs from `requested` or Yantra resolves model-indistinguishable choices structurally.     |
| `editee`     | The control the engine actually edited, present only when the page routed the edit to a different control.                           |

`resolution` is one of `exact` (the control holds what was asked for), `single_offered_match` (the widget offered one match and committed it), `selected_from_offered` (several were offered and one ranked uniquely), `typed_literal` (nothing matched, so the typed text stands), or `reformatted` (the control preserved the same letters and numbers while changing case, punctuation, or spacing, as an input mask may do). When a value came from the widget's own offered list, that choice is what the commit is verified against, not the text used to find it. A page rewrite to unrelated text is never accepted as `reformatted`: the typing ladder finishes, then the fill fails with the observed value and its complete attempt ledger.

The agent-facing guidance for `do` states this contract directly: a successful result whose `committed` value differs from what was sent is backed by an offered selection or a formatting-equivalent rewrite and must be accepted rather than re-filled; an `editee` means the value landed in a control the page chose, so the named field staying empty is expected; `attempted` is an ordered list of recovery verdicts, each read by its `verdict` — `succeeded` and `failed` name steps the tool already performed and must not be repeated, while a `skipped` entry names a step the tool did **not** take and says why in `unmet`, which is information rather than a prohibition; when `offered` is present, one of its labels can be re-issued verbatim through the interaction family that emitted it; a batch's `applied` fields are set and must not be re-sent; and a `skipped` field waits for the field named in its `blocked_by`. That guidance lives in the command's completion criteria and the tool descriptions, never in the governed system prompt, so `prompt_version` is unchanged and only `tool_catalog_hash` moves.

`browser_click` owns one bounded declarative plan. When the page replaces the node behind a ref mid-click, the tool re-observes and finds the element again — constrained to the same accessible name **and** role it described before the click, and refusing anything ambiguous, because recovering an identity is not the same as choosing a different control. The shared recovery runner executes that plan on one deadline and action allowance, so `resolved_by: "re-resolved"` and `attempted` account for the recovery that actually occurred. A click that simply worked reports neither. A disabled element is a definite answer and is never retried. No new pass/fail gate was added: a click that legitimately changes nothing visible still succeeds.

**A click or fill that cannot reach its target says so instead of hitting whatever is on top.** Chrome computes a click point from an element's content quads and dispatches there without asking what is topmost, so a click on a control under a consent modal used to land on the modal and return `ok` with a fresh observation — a silent false success on the most-used tool. Every pointer-dependent action now scrolls and settles as before, then proves the exact point Chrome would use belongs to the requested control, and dispatches at that same point.

When it does not, the action fails with `ELEMENT_OBSTRUCTED` — never `ELEMENT_HIDDEN`, because a covered element is visible and re-observing is not the fix. The failure names what is covering the control in structural terms only (a modal dialog, a busy indicator, a viewport-pinned fixed or sticky overlay, or a plain stacking overlay), the overlay's accessible name, and any dismiss controls found **inside that overlay's own subtree**, offered as ordinary `eNN` refs a `browser_click` can act on. A "Close" button elsewhere on the page is not that overlay's dismiss control and is never offered. Nothing in this decision consults a site, brand, or host.

At most one dismissal is pressed automatically, once per tool call — shared across every field and every typing rung of a `browser_fill_form`, so a batch cannot press its way through a page one field at a time — and only for a control whose label is an unambiguous dismissal (close, dismiss, decline, reject, no thanks, not now, maybe later, skip). Consent acceptances, navigation, submissions, purchases, and unlabelled icon-only controls are never pressed; neither is anything matching the protected-action shapes that already require your confirmation. The original point is re-tested after the press: if it worked the action proceeds normally, and if it did not the report says so rather than trying again. A busy indicator is never dismissed at all — it is transient, and the existing bounded retry waits it out.

A native `<select>` is filled by value rather than by pointer, so it is unaffected. Overlay names reaching the model or the run log pass the same sanitizer as any other page-derived text.

**A field is driven by the widget driver most confident about it, with fallback.** Detection is a guess made from the control's closed state, and a wrong guess used to end the attempt: a read-only trigger whose accessible name contains "date" was handed to the driver that types into date inputs, which typed into a control that cannot be typed into and stopped there — while the calendar driver that would have paged to the requested month was never consulted. Drivers are now ordered by their own confidence and tried in turn, falling through when one turns out to be wrong about itself. A definite answer from the page — a disabled date, a calendar that disagrees with its own weekday headers — stops the chain immediately rather than asking a second driver the same question. When more than one driver was tried, `attempted` names each one and why it was abandoned.

**A suggestion control is driven by a combobox driver that finds the real editee and shapes its own query.** Two things used to be fixed while only the typing mechanism varied, and both are common: the control the caller names is not always the one the page edits, and the text that was typed is not always a question the widget will answer.

- **Where the keystrokes go.** A trigger that opens an overlay and forwards typing to the overlay's own input stays empty however it is typed into. After the first entry mechanism leaves the control empty, the engine compares the page before and after and finds which control's value now holds the text. Exactly one match re-targets the fill to that control; two matches, or none, are never guessed at. When the fill re-targeted, the result carries `editee` naming the control that was actually edited — the value landed, and the field the caller named is not the place to look for it.
- **What the widget is asked.** One ordered plan per fill: the value as given, then a short uppercase code the request already carries, then a shortened leading prefix. The driver walks the plan and stops at the first form that produces suggestions. **Ranking is always against the full requested value, never against the shortened text that was typed**, so a list that only matches leading characters can be queried with a prefix and still resolved to the entry the caller asked for.

Because each emitting family has its own receiving path, a result telling the agent to "re-issue with one of those strings exactly as written" names a move the engine can actually make. A combobox can type a distinguishing prefix and select the matching entry; option and plain-text paths rank the re-issued label directly; and an engine-minted calendar label is routed back through the date family before ordinary date parsing. Capability-bearing advice is gated per emitting interaction family, so a message cannot name a retry that only some other family knows how to receive.

A control carrying none of the combobox signals — no `role="combobox"`, no `aria-autocomplete`, no popup it declares — is untouched by this and keeps the plain text path, including its own offered-list discovery.

**A picker that only reveals itself on click is opened and driven by the engine.** Widget detection reads a control's closed state and never clicks — that is what makes it safe to run every driver against every control. But a bare text box that mounts its calendar on click carries no popup attribute, no format hint and no rendered date, so every date driver correctly scores it zero and the fill used to fail outright. The agent's answer to that failure was to operate the calendar itself with a dozen `browser_click` calls.

So the click belongs to a separate stage the engine owns. It runs only when no driver recognised the control **and** the field's own shape agrees with what is being asked of it — a date asked of a text-like or date-named control, an option asked of a control that declares it opens something. It clicks once, re-runs detection against the container that appeared, and then either drives it or closes it again and fails carrying what it actually saw (`containerResolved`, `cellsSeen`, `optionsSeen`, `monthsSeen`). One probe per fill, recorded in `attempted` as `open-probe` followed by the driver it revealed.

**Operating a calendar or a dropdown with `browser_click` is never required.**

When several surviving choices have distinct model-visible labels and still match equally well, the engine picks none of them: it releases the popup and fails with `WIDGET_AMBIGUOUS_CHOICE` carrying pairwise-distinct `offered` labels, so the caller re-issues with the one it wants. Committing a guess would look like success while filling the wrong value.

When the surviving labels are indistinguishable, asking the model to choose would be impossible. Yantra instead narrows within the already-resolved container, prefers enabled and visible choices and a choice the page marks selected, then takes the first remaining choice in document order. That substitution is disclosed even when the committed value exactly matches the request: `note` names the shared label, and `attempted` records the indistinguishable count, selected position, and structural tie-break without copying the page label into the ledger. If more than one choice survives structural narrowing and their model-visible labels differ, Yantra does not collapse them.

An offered list is a menu, not a dump of everything clickable in a popup. When a container declares option roles, only those options qualify; paging, navigation, mode-switching, and other container chrome are scoped out. A protected-action label is vetoed from ranking, clicking, and every `offered` payload even in containers that rely on the fallback choice shape. If a failed container has no declared option semantics, the result omits `offered` and tells the caller to re-observe instead of advertising its incidental buttons as choices. Successful fallback selection remains supported for widgets that commit a real choice without declaring ARIA list semantics.

When nothing matches, whether typed text stands is read from the page rather than assumed — text the control keeps becomes the value (`typed_literal`), and a control that discards it on release is reported unreachable, with `offered` included only when genuine choices are available.

**An option list that mounts only the rows in its viewport is scrolled to reveal the requested option.** The engine advances the list's **own** scroll container, never the page or window, and only when the window it already collected failed to rank a match — a list whose target is already mounted is charged no scroll at all. At most `maxScrollSteps` steps are taken (eight by default), each charged against the same widget action budget and the same widget deadline as clicks and keystrokes, and the scan stops at the first of a match, a window that offers nothing new, a container that does not move, no scrollable region, the step cap, or the budget. A list that genuinely does not hold the value still fails with `WIDGET_TARGET_UNREACHABLE` / `value-not-offered`, carrying distinct, genuine `offered` evidence deduplicated across every window that was mounted rather than the first window's rows alone; its next step names re-issuing one of those labels because the option family can rank that label directly. When a scroll was charged to reach the choice, the result's `attempted` carries one `scroll-container` verdict on the `what` axis — that rung varies what the widget has been given a chance to offer, changing neither the target node nor the typing mechanics — holding the bounded scroll count and a structural stop token, never page text.

Failures carry the same kind of disclosure: `observed` is what the control holds right now, `offered`, when present, is the distinct set of genuine choices the widget will actually accept, and `attempted` lists the recovery the engine already performed — a typing ladder that escalated through three entry mechanisms, a re-target to the control the page really edits, or a driver fallback that tried two widget drivers. Work a `succeeded` or `failed` entry names has already been performed, so repeating it cannot succeed.

Each `attempted` entry is one verdict in an ordered sequence, carrying its `ordinal`, the `strategy` that ran, the recovery `axis` that strategy varies, and its `verdict`. `succeeded` and `failed` record work the tool actually performed, and `failed` carries the stable `error_code`. `skipped` is the opposite kind of fact: it names a step that was **not** taken, gives the structural condition that was not met in `unmet`, and spends no page work — a step to know about, not a step that is off limits. A key that would say nothing is omitted rather than written empty, so `error_code` appears only on a failure, `unmet` only on a skip, and `entry_evidence`, `charged_actions`, `remaining_actions`, and `elapsed_ms` only where they hold something — never as `[]` or `0` on every record. At most 24 records reach the model; a run that produces more keeps the first and the last 23, leaving the gap visible in the retained ordinals. The engine emits this projection once and both fill tools pass it through unchanged, so what a result shows is the ledger the runner recorded. Audit and report readers still accept the previous nullable record shape without rewriting old run directories.

**A failure's next step is specific to why it happened, and names only moves the engine can actually make.** The stable `error_code` is unchanged and remains the programmatic contract, but one code covers several unrelated situations: a control that took no keystrokes at all, one that took them and cleared them when the widget closed, and one that routed them into a different node are all `WIDGET_NOT_COMMITTED`. The message and next step are now selected by the code _and_ the reason together, so two failures sharing a code no longer read identically.

These properties are enforced mechanically rather than reviewed. Each next step declares the detail keys its wording refers to, and a test asserts they are populated wherever that failure is constructed — an instruction to "check details.displayedMonths" on a failure carrying no months is a build failure, not a wording problem. Every `offered`-bearing hint receives pairwise-distinct labels and may quote only labels in that payload. Each next step that asks for a _retry_ declares the engine capability that makes it work, and the gate resolves a concrete receiver for every interaction family allowed to emit it; there is no generic fallback sentence for a situation nobody wrote advice for.

Single-field recovery also keeps one absolute 25-second widget deadline and one action allowance across the initial drive, field re-resolution, and the second drive. Re-resolving a replaced field does not restart the clock. One `browser_fill_element` call is one run: the field plan and every fill it drives share a single 32-action ceiling, a single deadline, a single stale-ref reacquisition cap of four, and a single ordered verdict sequence, so a retry after an expensive first attempt gets no fresh allowance of its own. `browser_fill_form` drives each field as its own run, and each failed field carries its own ledger. Either way the result combines the outer `fill` / `re-resolve-field-and-retry` verdicts with the typing and driver work underneath them, so success and failure expose one complete ledger for the bounded operation.

**A browser that will not start is a distinct, final answer rather than a generic tool fault.** Chrome opens lazily, on the first tool call that needs a page, so a "no usable browser" condition surfaces inside a tool: `browser_navigate` on a run's first navigation, and `web_fetch` when a script-rendered or bot-refused page escalates the HTTP fetch to the browser fallback. Both boundaries report the local cause under a stable code with a message written for that cause:

| Code                           | Cause                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `BROWSER_RESOLUTION_FAILED`    | No usable Chrome or Chromium could be resolved on this machine.                                                 |
| `BROWSER_COMPATIBILITY_FAILED` | The local browser is missing an automation primitive Yantra requires, so it was refused before any page opened. |
| `BROWSER_COORDINATION_FAILED`  | The Yantra-managed browser is claimed by another Yantra browser operation, so this run could not reserve it.    |
| `BROWSER_LAUNCH_FAILED`        | The browser could not be started.                                                                               |
| `BROWSER_PROCESS_FAILED`       | The browser process could not be accounted for, so the run will not use it.                                     |
| `BROWSER_INSTALL_DECLINED`     | The user declined the offer to download a Yantra-managed browser.                                               |
| `BROWSER_INSTALL_FAILED`       | Installing the Yantra-managed browser did not complete.                                                         |

Every one of them is non-retryable: nothing in a run installs or repairs a browser, so an identical retry cannot succeed, and each message tells the agent to report the local remediation — installing a browser, `yantra browser install`, `yantra browser check`, `yantra doctor`, or waiting for the other operation to finish — and then finish with `result_publish` using the evidence it already has. It names no browser-management capability the agent itself possesses, because it has none.

The model sees the code, that message, and `retryable: false`. The sanitized `details` recorded in the run's tool audit carry the closed structural evidence — the resolution code and selected source, the compatibility failure class, probe profile, browser version and failing capability ids, the coordination reason, the launch or process phase and whether the exit was proven, or the managed-install code and phase. Launch arguments, helper output, executable and profile paths, and raw error text are never among them. Each result also carries a `failure_class` detail, `environment` for the six environment causes and `user-handoff` with `handoff: true` for a declined install, so audit and downstream orchestration keep the distinction between a broken local environment and a decision the user made.

These codes cover browser startup only. An ordinary site or navigation fault is still reported to the model as the generic, retryable `TOOL_EXECUTION_FAILED`, and `web_fetch`'s own `FETCH_TIMEOUT`, `CONTENT_TOO_LARGE`, `FETCH_HTTP_ERROR`, `FETCH_FAILED`, `CONTENT_TYPE_REFUSED`, and `EXTRACTION_EMPTY` results, along with its ethics refusals, are unaffected.

**A failed web search says why, names the provider, and offers one move the agent can actually make.** Every `web_search` provider failure maps through one ordered table to a stable code, and a failure to resolve the configured provider is classified the same way and is never reported as retryable. The model-visible message names the provider, says whether a retry can help, and gives one next step: search once more, `web_fetch` a URL an earlier result already returned, or finish with `result_publish`. Setup commands such as `yantra init` appear only as advice for the agent to relay to the user; nothing in a run can add a key or change the provider.

| Code                          | When                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Retryable |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| `SEARCH_BLOCKED`              | The provider served an anti-bot challenge instead of results, or rejected the search because its rate limit was reached. Every later search in the run also returns this code, with cause `circuit-open`, without being sent.   | No        |
| `SEARCH_NO_RESULTS`           | The search itself worked and returned nothing. The agent is told to reformulate the query once and, if that also returns nothing, to publish and say so.                                                                        | Yes       |
| `SEARCH_TIMEOUT`              | The search timed out before results arrived.                                                                                                                                                                                    | Yes       |
| `SEARCH_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE` | Yantra's ethics policy refused the provider's search page, the provider needs an API key that is not configured, no configured provider is usable, the configured provider is not recognized, or the provider rejected the key. | No        |
|                               | The provider returned a server (5xx) error.                                                                                                                                                                                     | Yes       |
| `SEARCH_FAILED`               | Loading the provider's results page failed before any results could be read.                                                                                                                                                    | Yes       |
|                               | The provider refused the request (4xx), answered with a response Yantra could not read, the search was cancelled, or the failure could not be classified.                                                                       | No        |

A scraped provider whose results-page browser cannot start returns the browser startup code from the table above, with that table's message, rather than a search code. The result's `details` carry the provider name and a closed cause token, never the provider's own error text.

**Reads skipped by the run's own budget are reported once, never as the sites' fault.** A successful `web_search` returns `sites` it read and per-site `failures`, each with a `stage`. When the run's navigation or distinct-host budget refuses a hit's read, that hit appears in neither list and is never reported as `blocked`; instead, the result's top-level `budget` object, which always carries the run's budget meter (see below), gains three fields:

| Field           | Meaning                                                                                          |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `exhausted`     | The limit that refused the reads, `navigations` or `hosts`. With both spent, the first is named. |
| `skipped_reads` | How many hits were not read, summed across limits.                                               |
| `message`       | Fixed wording that names the limit and the count, as below.                                      |

> Yantra's own navigation budget for this run is spent, so 3 further search result(s) were not read. This is the run limit, not the sites refusing you, and searching again cannot read more pages. Finish with result_publish now; the evidence already gathered is attached automatically.

For the host limit the message says `distinct-host` in place of `navigation`. Any other URL-policy refusal of a hit is a per-site failure with stage `policy`; only an ethics refusal or a challenge page is stage `blocked`. Neither a budget nor a policy refusal counts against that site's ranking, because the run's own limits refused the read, not the site.

**A page is read at most once per run, and keeps one evidence ID.** Every `web_fetch` and every page `web_search` reads inline goes through the run's document store. Two URLs name the same page when they match after the host is lowercased, the fragment, common tracking parameters such as `utm_*`, `gclid`, and `fbclid`, one trailing slash on a non-root path, and the default port are removed. So `https://Example.com:443/a/?utm_source=x#top` and `https://example.com/a` are one page. A page a read was redirected to also counts as read.

- The first successful read of a page assigns it a run-wide evidence ID, `S1`, `S2`, and so on in the order pages were first read. A failed read assigns nothing, so the numbers have no gaps. The same ID appears in `web_search` sites, `web_fetch` results, `browser_extract` results, and the run's evidence ledger. `web_search` sites carry `source_id` in place of the per-call number `n` they used to carry.
- A later `web_fetch` of a page already read, whether it was read by `web_fetch`, as a search hit, or as a redirect target, succeeds with `already_read` and `source_id` set to that ID, plus `url`, `title`, `capture_ref` when the content was stored as a capture, and a `note` saying the content was returned earlier under that ID. It carries no `text`, fetches nothing, and charges no navigation. The one exception is a page `web_search` showed only as a summary: the first `web_fetch` of it returns the full view from the store instead, as described below. In `web_search`, a hit already read appears in `sites` as `{source_id, url, title, already_read: true}` with no text.
- Two reads of the same page at the same moment share one fetch.
- A read that failed for a reason that cannot change within the run is not attempted again. Those reasons are an HTTP 4xx other than 408 and 429, a body over the size limit, a refused content type, a page with no extractable content, a robots or blocklist refusal, and a challenge page. A later `web_fetch` of that URL returns the original error code with a message saying the URL was already attempted and failed, `retryable: false`, and `details.already_attempted: true`; in `web_search` the hit is listed again as a per-site failure. Neither fetches anything. Timeouts, network errors, 5xx, 408, 429, rate-limit refusals, and budget refusals are not remembered, so a later read tries again.
- A `browser_extract` of any kind on an `http(s)` page reports that page's `source_id`. It reuses the ID when the page was already read and otherwise assigns one, without fetching anything. It always returns the live page's content and is never `already_read`. A page with no `http(s)` URL, such as `about:blank`, gets no ID and records nothing.

**`web_search` with `limit: 0` only discovers.** `limit` accepts 0 through 5 and is also bounded by `search.fetch_top`. With `0`, the provider is asked as usual, and the result is `{query, mode: "discovery", results: [{url, title, snippet}], note}`, with no `sites`, `failures`, or `more_results`. Nothing is fetched, no navigation is charged, no per-hit ethics check runs, and no browser starts beyond the provider's own results page when the provider is a scraped one. Every listed URL is attested, so the agent may `web_fetch` it; the note says snippets are not page content and to call `web_fetch` with a URL exactly as listed.

**Every page read reports what kind of page it is and returns the data that kind of page holds.** A successful `web_fetch` returns `source_id`, `url`, `title`, and a `shape`: `article`, `collection` (a listing or results page), `table`, `detail` (one item's attributes, such as a product page), or `index` (a hub with no content of its own but links to follow). The part the shape leads with comes next: `text` for an article, `records` for a collection, `tables` for a table page, `fields` for a detail page, and `links` for an index page. The page's other parts follow in a fixed order (`fields`, `tables`, `structured`, `records`, `links`, then `text`), and `coverage` comes last. A part the page does not have is omitted.

| Field        | Contents                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `records`    | Up to 25 repeated items. Each has an `id` such as `S3#r5`, a `title`, its primary `url`, `text` (its text runs in page order, linked text included), up to 8 `fields`, up to 6 typed `numbers` (`currency`, `distance`, or `count`), and up to 3 secondary `links`, such as a seller's page. Each record holds at most 400 characters of text. |
| `tables`     | Every table, up to 10, as `{index, kind, caption, headers, rows}`. `index` is the table's 0-based position among all tables on the page in document order, nested tables included. `kind` is `data`, `key-value`, or `layout`; a layout table has no rows. At most 50 rows, 20 columns, and 200 characters per cell.                           |
| `fields`     | Up to 60 page-level label/value pairs from definition lists, two-column tables, and "Label: value" lines, as an object. A repeated label gets a ` (2)` suffix.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `structured` | Up to 25 schema.org entities from JSON-LD or microdata, as `{type, from, props}`. Nested properties are flattened to dotted keys such as `offers.price` or `offers.0.seller.name`.                                                                                                                                                             |
| `links`      | Up to 40 links the page offers, as `{text, url, kind}`, deduplicated and ranked by kind (`pagination`, `facet`, `content`, then `navigation`) and then same-site first. A record's primary link appears in `records`, not here.                                                                                                                |
| `text`       | The article text when the page has one, otherwise the page's visible text in blocks. On an article page it is byte-identical to what the article extractor returns for that page, and the result also carries `byline` and `published_at`.                                                                                                     |
| `coverage`   | Per part, what was `found` and `shown`; `shape_basis`, one sentence naming why the shape beat the runner-up; `fetch_mode`; `not_found`, fixed phrases for what was looked for and absent, such as `no repeated records`; and `omitted`, one fixed sentence per bound that dropped data.                                                        |

A record keeps its ID for the whole run. When the same page is read again, for example by `browser_extract` after the page changed, a record already seen keeps its number and a new record gets the next one. Each `omitted` sentence names the engineered way to the rest, or says plainly that none exists: records beyond the first 25 can be reached only through a `pagination` link the page offers. A page with no readable content, no page parts, and no link to follow still fails with `EXTRACTION_EMPTY`, and its message lists what was looked for.

A full view is kept within 90% of the per-result byte budget. When it does not fit, it shrinks in a fixed order: `text` becomes a 1,000-character `excerpt` plus a `capture_ref`, `links` are cut to 20 and then 10, and then structured entities, table rows, and records are dropped from the end, one at a time. Every trim adds a sentence to `coverage.omitted`, and the full analysis is written once to the run's `captures/` directory, so nothing is lost from the run directory. No tool reads a capture back.

The evidence ledger's excerpt for a page follows its shape: an article's excerpt, a collection's first three records, a detail page's fields, a table page's first table, or an index page's text, at most 1,000 characters.

**A search shows each non-article site as a summary, and the full view is one store read away.** In `web_search`, a site whose page is not an article carries its `source_id`, `url`, `title`, `shape`, up to 5 `records`, up to 10 `pagination` and `facet` links, a 1,000-character `excerpt`, `coverage`, and a `note` saying that `web_fetch` of the URL returns the full view without a new fetch. The first `web_fetch` of that URL returns the full view from the run's store with `from_store: true`. It fetches nothing, charges no navigation, and does not add the page to the evidence ledger a second time. A later `web_fetch` is `already_read`. An article site keeps its `text`, or a `capture_ref`, and its `excerpt`, and gains `shape` and `coverage`; it is already delivered in full, so a `web_fetch` of it is `already_read`.

**`browser_extract` reads the live page through the same analyzer.** Every kind except `content` takes one snapshot of the rendered page and runs it through the analyzer `web_fetch` uses, so a record, link, or table means the same thing on both paths:

| `kind`               | Returns                                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `content` (default)  | The rendered `title` and readable `text`, with paragraph breaks kept.                                                                                                        |
| `records`            | The page's records, with their `S<n>#r<k>` IDs.                                                                                                                              |
| `links`              | Up to 40 links: `pagination` and `facet` links first, then each record's primary link with kind `record`, then the rest.                                                     |
| `structured`         | The page's schema.org entities.                                                                                                                                              |
| `tables`             | Every table.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `table` with `index` | One table by its 0-based position. An index past the last table returns `INVALID_INPUT` saying how many tables the page has, and the call can be retried with a valid index. |

`listings`, `items`, and `results` resolve to `records`; `urls` to `links`; `json_ld` and `schema` to `structured`; and `first_table` to `table` with index 0. An unsupported kind returns `INVALID_INPUT` with a message that lists every kind and when to use it. Every kind except `content` returns `source_id`, `url`, `title`, `shape`, the requested part, and `coverage`. Every kind except `links` records the page as evidence. A snapshot that is a human-verification page returns `SITE_CHALLENGE` with `handoff: true` and records no evidence and no links.

**Links a page offers can be followed.** Every URL a read shows the model becomes navigable for `web_fetch` and `browser_navigate`, attributed to the page that offered it: a link in `links[]`, a record's `url` or secondary link, a URL property in `structured`, or a URL written in returned `text` or `excerpt`. A URL is shown only when the sanitizer leaves it byte-identical, so the URL copied is exactly the URL that was recorded; any other URL is shown as `url: null` and counted in `coverage.links.withheld`. A URL no search result, page read, or goal attested is refused with `URL_NOT_FROM_EVIDENCE` before anything is fetched or charged. See [Discovered-link provenance](safety-and-privacy.md#discovered-link-provenance).

For example, a goal that asks for the colors of the top vehicles in a filtered listing can be completed entirely from offered moves:

1. `web_search` with `limit: 0` lists the listing's results-page URL without fetching it.
2. `web_fetch` of that URL returns `shape: "collection"` as `S1`, with records `S1#r1` through `S1#r6`, each carrying a title, price, seller, distance, and detail link. Its `links[]` include the drivetrain filter values as `facet` links and the next pages as `pagination` links.
3. `web_fetch` of the facet link's `url`, copied exactly, reads the filtered listing. The call's audit record says the URL was `discovered` via `S1` with link kind `facet`.
4. `web_fetch` of a record's `url` returns `shape: "detail"` with `fields` such as `Exterior color` and `Interior color`.
5. A detail URL the agent builds itself, for example by changing the identifier in a record's URL, is refused with `URL_NOT_FROM_EVIDENCE`, and no request reaches the site.

`run-health.json` counts the successful follows in steps 3 and 4 as `discovered_follows`.

**Every evidence result shows the run's budget.** Every successful `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `browser_navigate`, and `browser_extract` result carries `budget: {navigations: "<used>/<limit>", hosts: "<used>/<limit>"}`, for example `{"navigations": "2/30", "hosts": "1/20"}`, read when the result is returned. An unbounded limit reads `∞`. The meter counts toward the result's size like any other field, and failures carry none. A navigation is charged only when a network fetch is actually attempted, after the ethics check, or by `browser_navigate`; a repeat read, a remembered failure, and a discovery search charge nothing.

**Searches are paced, and stop after the provider's first challenge.** A run resolves its search provider once. A scraped provider (`google`, `duckduckgo`) is asked one query at a time, each started at least 2 seconds after the previous one started; a keyed API provider (`brave`, `tavily`) takes two queries at once with no spacing. Additional searches wait their turn, and a search cancelled while waiting is never sent. The first anti-bot challenge or rate-limit refusal is reported as `SEARCH_BLOCKED` with its own cause and closes search for the rest of the run. Every later `web_search`, including one already waiting its turn, returns `SEARCH_BLOCKED` with cause `circuit-open` at once, without asking the provider or starting a browser. Its message says search is closed for the rest of the run and offers `web_fetch` of a URL an earlier result returned, or `result_publish`. Yantra does not switch to another provider.

**The search result says when another search is useful.** A `web_search` result's `note` reads: "These sites are recorded as your sources automatically, each under its source_id. Publish with result_publish when the evidence answers the goal. Search again only for a different part of the goal or to locate a source the goal requires — do not re-run a search you already ran, and do not re-type URLs." It adds "To go deeper into a site above, follow its links[] or records[]." only when at least one returned site carries links or records. A `limit: 0` discovery result's note is the discovery note (titles, URLs, and snippets only; call `web_fetch` with a URL exactly as listed to read it) followed by the same "Search again only…" sentence.

**A human-verification page is never read as content.** Every response a `web_fetch` or a `web_search` inline read receives is classified before extraction. When Yantra's HTTP client gets a challenge page, the URL is rendered once in the standard headless browser, with no retry and no change to the browser's identity. When that render, or any render the fetch escalated to, is also a challenge page, the read fails:

- `web_fetch` returns `SITE_CHALLENGE` with `retryable: false` and `details: {host, tier, handoff: true}`. The message says the host served a human-verification page, that Yantra cannot and will not pass it and will not request the page again in this run, and to use evidence from other reads or finish with `result_publish` saying the page was blocked.
- In `web_search`, the hit is a per-site failure with stage `blocked` and reason `challenge page (<marker>)`.

The page is never extracted, never becomes a source, and is not fetched again in the run. A run that ends without publishing after a `SITE_CHALLENGE` is a user handoff. See [Challenge pages](safety-and-privacy.md#challenge-pages) for the markers and the signed-off policy.

The run completes only with a schema-valid publication. If the model stops with prose instead, Yantra sends one publication nudge and freezes further web evidence gathering when evidence already exists. If the model still does not publish but Yantra has both a draft and evidence, the runtime packages them into a validated Brief marked as a deterministic fallback. That fallback preserves resolvable inline evidence-ID citations, removes numeric and unresolved citation markers, and reports contract gaps as notices. It does not infer a missing table from draft prose. Without both draft and evidence, the run fails with `AGENT_COMPLETION_MISSING` and preserves the final sanitized prose as diagnostic `result.md`.

**The repeated-failure breaker counts identical failures per tool.** `--tool-retries <n>` (default 3) is not a retry count: Yantra never retries a tool call on the agent's behalf. It bounds identical failures of one tool. When the same tool fails with the same error `n + 1` times with no success of that tool in between, the run stops as a repeated tool failure. A success of that tool resets its count, a different error code restarts it at 1, and other tools' outcomes never touch it, so an alternating "observe succeeds, click fails" loop still trips the breaker. Denied and aborted calls are not counted, and a `TOOL_TIMEOUT` that lands after the 80% wind-down has begun does not trip it, so the agent can still publish. The per-run prompt states the rule as "repeated identical failures: a tool failing with the same error N times without succeeding in between stops the run", where N is `n + 1`.

### Task contract

`research` and `do` register a `task_contract` tool; `ask` does not. The agent uses it to record what the user's goal requires before it gathers evidence:

| Field              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deliverable`      | `table` (rows with the same fields each), `answer`, or `report`.                                                                                               |
| `subject`          | What the rows or the answer are about (1–200 characters).                                                                                                      |
| `required_fields`  | Every field the goal asks for (up to 12). Required, and non-empty, for a `table`.                                                                              |
| `filters`          | Every condition the goal states, as `{name, value}` pairs (up to 12).                                                                                          |
| `required_sources` | Every site the goal names, as a hostname (up to 5). Each entry is normalized: lowercased, with scheme, path, port, trailing dot, and a leading `www.` removed. |
| `ranking`          | Optional `{field, direction}` (`asc` or `desc`). For a table, `field` must be one of `required_fields`.                                                        |
| `limit`            | Optional number of results the goal asks for (1–50).                                                                                                           |
| `notes`            | Optional free text (up to 500 characters) for anything the fields cannot express, such as a site named without its address.                                    |

Declaring a contract is optional: it fetches nothing, grants nothing, and no other tool requires it. The guidance asks the agent to call it in the same turn as its first search or fetch, so it costs no extra turn, and to call it again with the full corrected contract only if a later result shows the goal was misread. Every string is passed through the run's sanitizer (`public` profile), marked user values are masked back to their placeholders, and control characters are stripped before the contract is stored, written, echoed, or logged. Names are compared ignoring case.

A call fails, and nothing is recorded, in these cases:

| Code                      | Cause                    | When                                                                                         |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `INVALID_INPUT`           | `contract-source-host`   | A `required_sources` entry is not a site address; the message names it and suggests `notes`. |
| `INVALID_INPUT`           | `contract-duplicate`     | A field, filter name, or source appears twice.                                               |
| `INVALID_INPUT`           | `contract-table-fields`  | A `table` contract has no `required_fields`.                                                 |
| `INVALID_INPUT`           | `contract-ranking-field` | A table's `ranking.field` is not one of its `required_fields`.                               |
| `CONTRACT_REVISION_LIMIT` | `revisions`              | Three revisions were already declared. Not retryable.                                        |
| `ACTION_PHASE_CLOSED`     | `published`              | The result was already published. Not retryable.                                             |

Only the first problem is reported, so each failing call gets one cause-specific message. `INVALID_INPUT` is retryable with the corrected full contract.

A successful call returns `{revision, contract, note}` with the normalized contract, rewrites `<run-dir>/contract.json` with every revision so far (at most 3; the last is current), and writes one `contract_declared` line to `runtime.jsonl` (see [Run artifacts](diagnostics-and-audit.md#run-artifacts)). In a text-mode run the CLI then prints what the run understood to stderr, beside the goal echo, so a misreading is visible in the first seconds:

```text
understood: table of new SUV listings — fields: seller, price, exterior color, interior color; filters: drivetrain=AWD; sources: example.com
```

A later revision prints `understood (revised): …`. The summary is built only from the normalized contract, omits empty parts, has no newlines or control characters, and is at most 400 characters. `--json` instead emits the event as an `agent_progress` record with `type: "contract_declared"`, `revision`, `summary`, and `at`, so stdout stays machine-readable.

A `research` or `do` run that publishes without ever declaring a contract, including one whose only declaration failed, carries one Brief notice with kind `other` and source `task-contract`, reading exactly: "No task contract was declared, so the deliverable, required fields, filters, and required sources were not recorded for this run." It leads the runtime-derived notices described under [Inputs and Outputs](#inputs-and-outputs). An `ask` run never carries it.

The contract records what the run understood and is checked when agent content becomes a Brief. Its `required_sources` never make a URL navigable (see [Safety and privacy](safety-and-privacy.md#discovered-link-provenance)).

### Attributed publication

The agent calls `result_publish` with a `brief` containing `title` and `overview`, plus the structured content below. References are the IDs returned by this run's tools: `S3` names a page and `S3#r1` names a record on that page. Copy the actual IDs from tool results; an ID from another run cannot be cited.

| Field               | Content and limits                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `key_findings`      | Up to 20 plain strings or `{text, sources: ["S3"]}` objects. A finding with no references is editorial commentary.                                                                           |
| `sections`          | Up to 8 `{heading, body_md, sources}` objects; headings are at most 120 characters, bodies 4,000 characters.                                                                                 |
| `table`             | `{columns, rows, row_sources}` with 1–12 columns and 1–50 rows. Column names are at most 60 characters; cells contain strings (at most 300 characters), finite numbers, booleans, or `null`. |
| `table.row_sources` | One non-empty reference list for each row, in the same order. Each row must have exactly as many cells as there are columns.                                                                 |
| `constraints`       | Up to 12 `{name, value, status, sources}` objects. Status is `verified`, `unverified`, or `violated`; names and values are at most 60 and 120 characters.                                    |
| `fulfillment`       | `{met, unmet: [{item, reason}]}` with up to 12 unmet items; item names are at most 80 characters and reasons 200 characters. Runtime checks still apply when `met` is `true`.                |

Reference lists accept up to 8 IDs. Overview, finding text, and section bodies also accept inline markers such as `[S3]` and `[S3#r1]`. Yantra resolves them into the document's numbered citations. Table references become `facets.comparison.row_citations`, and section and constraint references become their structured `citations` arrays in `brief.json`.

For example, after a read returned record ID `S3#r1`:

```json
{
  "brief": {
    "title": "Listings",
    "overview": "One listing was read [S3#r1].",
    "table": {
      "columns": ["Seller", "Price"],
      "rows": [["Example seller", 43204]],
      "row_sources": [["S3#r1"]]
    },
    "fulfillment": { "met": true, "unmet": [] }
  }
}
```

When the run has evidence, Yantra owns source URLs, titles, timestamps, and numbering; a model-supplied `sources` list cannot replace them. Sources referenced anywhere in the Brief, including its alternatives, receive `cited: true` and sort first. Other ledger entries receive `cited: false` and render under **Also consulted**. Multiple record references from one page share one numbered source. When the ledger is empty, a supplied source list still undergoes protocol validation. Complete protocol Briefs from internal callers and template reports use their existing publication paths; this evidence-ID composition applies to agent-content Briefs.

**The task contract shapes the answer.** A table contract requires a table and columns for its required fields, unless `fulfillment.unmet` names the missing table or field and explains why it could not be delivered. Field matching ignores case and punctuation and requires every field token in the column name; it does not equate `color` with `colour`. Empty or `null` required cells become `not shown on source`, with a contract-gap notice. This missing-data placeholder is excluded from anchoring checks.

Rows and cited findings with no reference to a required-source host or its subdomains move into an **Alternatives (not from …)** section, marked `kind: "alternatives"` in `brief.json`. A row with at least one required-source citation stays in the main table, even if it also cites another host. Uncited editorial findings stay commentary. The runtime adds notices when the answer has no cited required-source content or all table rows became alternatives; it does not silently merge alternatives into the requested answer.

Every contract filter appears in **Conditions**, beneath the title. An omitted condition is added as `unverified`; a condition marked `verified` without references is downgraded to `unverified`. Unverified and violated conditions, declared unmet items, and missing required cells produce `contract_gap` notices. These checks do not establish that the declared contract matches the original goal or enforce its ranking and result limit.

**Correctable errors leave publication open.** `BRIEF_INVALID` is retryable and returns all composition issues in `details.issues`, each with its `cause`, `pointer`, and corrective message. Causes include `reference-unknown`, `reference-anchor-unknown`, `reference-numeric` (use `[S3]` rather than `[3]` in agent prose), `row-uncited`, `row-width`, `row-sources-length`, `contract-table-missing`, and `contract-field-missing`. The agent can correct the payload and publish again. Exactly one successful publication closes the action phase.

**Anchoring flags unsupported values without deleting them.** A deterministic check compares each cited non-empty string or numeric table cell, cited finding, and verified condition against its referenced evidence. Record IDs use that record's evidence; page IDs use retained page content, or the ledger title and excerpt when page content is unavailable. It checks normalized numbers and word overlap; cited sections receive a numbers-only check. Missing values generate an `uncited_claim_flagged` notice and remain in the published answer. `metadata.citation_verdict` records `claims_checked`, `flagged`, and `stripped: 0`. This is a heuristic check of evidence presence, not proof of truth, entailment, units, or freshness.

Model-authored publication text passes the public sanitizer before composition. Marked user values remain masked during checking and resolve to their original values in the published artifact. A successful publication's tool response summarizes cited and consulted sources, main-table and alternative row counts, condition statuses, contract gaps, and flagged values. Its `brief_composed` entry in `runtime.jsonl` records counts only; cell text, page text, and URLs are excluded. The sanitized tool audit retains the publication parameters and their evidence references.

## How to Use It

Run a browser task:

```console
yantra do "find nonstop flights from Chicago to Seattle for September 6 through September 12"
```

Restrict all outbound work to user-approved hosts. Repeat `--allow-host` for more than one host:

```console
yantra do "compare these products and summarize the differences" \
  --allow-host example.com \
  --allow-host shop.example.net
```

Select a provider and model:

```console
yantra do "check whether the support form accepts my case" \
  --provider ollama \
  --model llama3.1:8b
```

Protect run-scoped values from the model while leaving them usable by tools:

```console
yantra do 'sign in to example.com as @username{demo-user} with @password{demo-password}'
```

Use a reusable report template:

```console
yantra do "prepare the launch review" --template ./templates/launch.md
```

Promote the successful browser trace to a saved workflow:

```console
yantra do "look up the current order status" --save-as order-status
yantra run order-status
```

Stream machine-readable progress and outcome records:

```console
yantra do "check the public status page" --json
```

`discover` is an alias for `do`.

### Options

| Option                         | Meaning                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--provider <name>`            | Select the model provider.                                                                                                                            |
| `--model <id>`                 | Select a provider-scoped model id.                                                                                                                    |
| `--thinking <level>`           | Request a supported provider reasoning level.                                                                                                         |
| `--auth-secret <ref>`          | Use an OS-keychain secret reference as a runtime-only model key.                                                                                      |
| `--max-duration <duration>`    | Set the hard wall-clock duration for the whole run.                                                                                                   |
| `--max-tokens <n>`             | Set the cumulative provider-token ceiling.                                                                                                            |
| `--tool-timeout <duration>`    | Set the timeout for one tool attempt.                                                                                                                 |
| `--tool-retries <n>`           | Bound identical failures of one tool: the run stops when one tool fails with the same error `n + 1` times without succeeding in between.              |
| `--confirm-timeout <duration>` | Set the maximum live consent wait.                                                                                                                    |
| `--allow-host <host>`          | Restrict outbound work to a host; repeatable. With no values, the run still follows URL provenance and host-budget rules.                             |
| `--save-as <name>`             | After successful publication, attempt to promote the browser trace to a saved workflow. Promotion failure does not change the successful run outcome. |
| `--template <name\|tag\|path>` | Render into a saved template, tag, or Markdown template path instead of the default Brief.                                                            |
| `--json`                       | Emit progress and the terminal outcome as newline-delimited JSON. It also makes the run non-interactive.                                              |
| `--no-llm`                     | Shared agent-option veto. `do` has no deterministic task executor, so this option exits with validation guidance instead of running the goal.         |

Durations are positive integers with an optional `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h` suffix; a bare integer means milliseconds. See [Shared flags and output behavior](../usage.md#shared-flags-and-output-behavior) for defaults, preference and environment equivalents, and precedence.

## Inputs and Outputs
